The firm does not maintain a 12-week register and the firm estimates 30% of the meal entertainment expenditure was provided to Smith as a fringe benefit. What should be the taxable value of meal entertainment fringe benefit in this scenario? Option A: $ 30,000 Option B: $ 27,000 Option C: $ 45,000 Option D: None of the above The correct answer is Option C.
reference: 30,000 * 50% = 15,000 * 30/70 = 75% * 30/70 = 45,000 Taxable Value = 90,000 * 30/70 = 45,000 Source - Barkoczy (2016), Foundation of Taxation Law (8th Edition) p. 534, Fringe Benefit Tax - Meal Entertainment(Topic 20) Textbook Page: 580 - 582 Paragraphs [FBTAA] - [FOTL] * Meal entertainment fringe benefit is given by the employer to the employee during the course of the work. * The taxable value of meal entertainment fringe benefit is calculated as 50% of the overall entertainment expenses. * The employer can claim deductions for the cost of providing meal entertainment fringe benefits to non-employee. * However, the taxable value of meal entertainment fringe benefit is reduced by any deductible amount that the employer could have claimed if it had been an employee. The FC of T contended that the amount received by the wife of a convicted person for services rendered to her husband while he was in gaol was an income nature. The wife entered the gaol as a visitor and provided her husband with various services including washing and mending his clothes and keeping his cell clean. The wife gave evidence that she did not charge for the services and that she was not sure how much she had saved the convicted person. The wife of the convicted person had been permitted by the prison authorities to act as a "housekeeper" in the gaol and was paid a small sum each week by the authorities. The wife had entered into a contract with the authorities where she undertook to provide the housekeeping services in return for which she was paid the small sum each week. input: Given question: Which of the following fringe benefit is taxable? Option A: De minimis benefit Option B: Benefits that are given to supervisory employees Option C: Benefits provided to rank and file employees Option D: Benefits given in the form of insurance or retirement benefits plan Option E: Benefits given to support employees education The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Fringe benefits tax regime is essentially a tax on a wide range of benefits provided by an employer to an employee. This tax is payable by the employer, not the employee, because the benefit is received from the employment. There are a number of different types of fringe benefit, which all fall within these two categories.In this case, the fringe benefit is taxable because it falls within one of these two categories. A de minimis benefit is a minor, trivial benefit that can be given to an employee without it being classified as a fringe benefit. It is called a de minimis benefit because the value of the benefit is so small that it is unimportant. In practice, de minimis benefits are usually related to the workplace, such as a birthday cake or a cup of coffee. They are not subject to FBT because they are not significant enough to constitute a benefit.A benefit that is given to supervisory employees is also taxable. These benefits are treated differently under the FBTAA because they are given to employees who have some level of responsibility for managing other employees.Benefits provided to rank and file employees are also taxable. These benefits are generally given to employees who do not have any level of responsibility for managing other employees.Benefits given in the form of insurance or retirement benefits plan are also taxable.An employer may provide an employee with a range of benefits from which the employee chooses the benefit that best suits the employee’s needs. For example, an employee might be able to choose between an additional week of annual leave and a one-off payment of $5000.The option e is the correct answer because it supports employees education. This is a taxable fringe benefit. Employers are encouraged to provide educational assistance to their employees because it helps to increase the skill levels of the workforce and improve productivity. However, if an employer pays for an employee to undertake a course of study, the benefit will be regarded as a taxable fringe benefit.  * Chapter 20, Fringe Benefit Tax, Foundations of Taxation Law (9th Edition), Stephen Barkoczy, 2017. source: Topic 8 Lecture Slides - Fringe Benefit Tax - Page 17 of 26 - Notional deduction slides. input: Given question: Under which circumstances a tax payers will not be able to deduct a debt which is written off in that particular income year ? Option A: It was not included in the taxpayer's assessable income for the income year or an earlier income year. Option B: Deductions are not available for debts that have been released, extinguished or compromised. Option C: A debt has gone bad when it is reasonably regarded as irrecoverable. Option D: A bad debt is deductible in year that it is physically written off in the tax payer's accounts. Option E: It is in respect of money lent by the tax payer in the ordinary course of a money lending business. The correct answer is Option A.
reference: Section 25-35 ITAA97 states that a tax payer will not be able to deduct a debt which is written off in that particular income year if it was not included in the taxpayer's assessable income for the income year or an earlier income year. A deduction cannot be claimed for a debt that has been released, extinguished or compromised. A debt has gone bad when it is reasonably regarded as irrecoverable. A bad debt is deductible in year that it is physically written off in the tax payer's accounts. In respect of money lent by the tax payer in the ordinary course of a money lending business is a valid deduction under s25-35 ITAA97. Option A: $12,500 Option B: $16,666 Option C: $12,000 Option D: $12,800 The correct answer is Option A.
reference: 12,500 - Annual amount required to be shown in assessable income = A(B-C)/D                               = (1($400,000 - $100,000))/24                               = $12,500 Where, A = taxpayer's share of annuity in relation to the year of income B = amount of the undeducted purchase price of the annuity C = residual capital value in relation to the annuity or nil D = relevant number in relation to the annuity (Barkoczy, 2017, p308) Topic 5 (Chapter 11)Statutory IncomeReference:Barkoczy, S. Option A: Compensation for loss of physical abilities generally fall into one of five categories of Compensation or damages received by an individual Option B: Depending on the nature of the payment, the compensation could be characterised as income or capital Option C: Compensation for substitution of lost salary or wages is NOT an ordinary income under the replacement principle (s 6-5). best_explanation: Compensation for substitution of lost salary or wages is an ordinary income under the replacement principle (s 6-5).  Structured settlements are often used to provide compensation for personal injuries. A structured settlement means a settlement of a claim for compensation or damages for personal injury where at least one part of the payment is an annuity. Annuities are normally assessable under s 27H ITAA36, but for certain allowances and payments, the payment of an annuity is regarded as having a capital aspect (s 27H(2) ITAA36). This means that the annuity is treated as capital and not income for tax purposes. This is because the annuity has been used to replace lost salary or wages, the compensation for which is assessable under the replacement principle (s 6-5). Therefore, the correct answer for C is Compensation for substitution of lost salary or wages is an ordinary income under the replacement principle (s 6-5).  The other statements are correct. input: Given question: Functions of AASB (Australian Accounting Standards Board) under s.227 of ASIC Act, includes the followings, EXCEPT, Option A: Promoting financial stability by leading institutions to manage risk prudently for minimizing losses to depositors, policy holders etc. Option B: Developing a conceptual framework Option C: Contributing for developing a single set of accounting standards for global use Option D: Formulating accounting standard that consist of law under s.334 of the Corporations Act Option E: Uplifting the significance of main objects of the financial reporting system part of the ASIC Act The correct answer is Option A.
reference: 1- Promoting financial stability by leading institutions to manage risk prudently for minimizing losses to depositors, policy holders etc. - This is the core objective of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC). 2- Developing a conceptual framework - The AASB develops conceptual frameworks for the purpose of accounting for transactions and events. 3- Contributing for developing a single set of accounting standards for global use - The AASB works towards achieving this objective through its involvement in the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). 4- Formulating accounting standard that consist of law under s.334 of the Corporations Act - The power to formulate accounting standards is vested in the AASB by s.227(1) of the ASIC Act. 5- Uplifting the significance of main objects of the financial reporting system part of the ASIC Act - The main object of the financial reporting system is to assist in the economic decision making process.The above are the functions of the AASB under s.227 of the ASIC Act, except for point 1 as it is the core objective of the ASIC. The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 1) An entity must “carry on an enterprise”: This requirement is derived from the Australian tax law concept of an “enterprise” which is defined in s 9-20 GST Act as “a business, profession, trade, employment, vocation or calling, but does not include a recreational pursuit or entertainment”. In Ruling TR 92/3, the Commissioner has indicated that the term “entertainment” should be interpreted restrictively and that an activity will not be entertainment if it contains a sufficient degree of pleasure or enjoyment to be regarded as a recreational pursuit. 2) The entity’s GST turnover is over the ‘registration turnover threshold’: The registration turnover threshold is $75,000 ($150,000 for non profit organisations).An entity may register for GST even if its GST turnover is below the registration turnover threshold if it carries on an enterprise. However, entities that carry on an enterprise must register for GST regardless of their turnover unless they are employees or certain other exclusions under Div 33. input: Given question: Which case illustrated the difficulty when distinguishing between annuities and installment payments for the fixed price of a capital asset? Option A: Smith v FCT 87 ATC 4883 Option B: FCT v Holmes 95 ATC 4476 Option C: Payne v FCT 96 ATC 4407 Option D: Australia and New Zealand Savings Bank Ltd v FCT 93 ATC 4370 Option E: IRC v Ramsay [1953] 1 All ER 847 The correct answer is Option E.
reference: The principle established by the Ramsay case has been followed in several subsequent cases. In FCT v Holmes 95 ATC 4476, it was held that where a taxpayer enters into an agreement to make periodic payments to another entity, the critical question is whether the payments are consideration for a transferable right to receive income or capital. In contrast, in Smith v FCT 87 ATC 4883, the court found that a lump sum payment with no conditions attached was a capital payment, even though there was some evidence of an intention to return the payments as an annuity. Similarly, in Payne v FCT 96 ATC 4407, the court held that a one-off payment was a capital payment, again because there was no condition attaching to the payment. By contrast, Australia and New Zealand Savings Bank Ltd v FCT 93 ATC 4370 involved a loan agreement which required the borrower to repay the loan in equal monthly instalments over a period of years. The agreement also contained a provision entitling the bank to require the borrower to immediately repay the loan if the borrower breached any of the other provisions of the agreement. It was held that the payments were part of the purchase price of the house and therefore capital in nature. This is because the payment is not broken down into smaller amounts that would constitute an annuity. 10.6 Apportionment Where a payment is made in lump sum but constitutes a proportion of an annuity then the payment must be apportioned. 10.7 Reduced term annuities A reduced term annuity is an annuity that pays out for a reduced number of years. reference: be used to overcome the deficiencies in the legislation. It helps in filling the legislative vacuums. Judicial precedent, also known as stare decisis, is the principle that courts should follow their own previous decisions. This allows for consistent interpretation and application of the law. Taxation law is no exception to this principle. It is interpreted based on the doctrine of precedent. This means that judicial precedent is an important source of tax law. Legislation may be incomplete or ambiguous. In such cases, the courts can refer to the legislative history, which includes things like the reports of parliamentary committees, to help fill legislative vacuums. This process of interpreting legislation involves consideration of a number of factors, including the words of the legislation, the purposes behind it and the intended beneficiaries. When interpreting legislation, the courts often look at the purpose behind it. They do this by considering the words of the legislation in the context of the problem it was designed to address. best_explanation: Source of income is from France where he renders services.  As a foreign resident, his source of income is from the place he works.  Even if he is a contractor, his source of income is from the place he works.  If he is on a project in France for 6 months, his source of income is from France.  The same applies to Mr. Chugh.  Hence, his source of income is from France.  Hence, France is the source of income.  Reference: Topic 3 - Source of income (Slide 4)   Mr. Chugh is a resident of India, who comes to Australia to work for a while. He enters into an agreement with a French company to do some work in France for six months. He goes to France and completes the work. The income he receives from the French company for the work he does in France will be income derived in France and will be taxable in France. As a temporary resident of France he would be required to pay tax at the prevailing French rates. If he were a resident of France he would be entitled to the tax-free allowance. He would not be required to pay Australian tax on this income. He would, however, be required to pay Australian tax on any income he received from Australian sources. If he has not been a resident of Australia for more than 183 days he will not be entitled to the tax-free allowance. If he has been a resident of Australia for more than 183 days he will be entitled to the tax-free allowance on his ordinary income. He will still not be required to pay Australian tax on the income he received from French sources. input: Given question: Who pays tax on a partnership business? Option A: Partnership Option B: The individual Partners Option C: Both Option D: None of the Above Option E: Non-Partner The correct answer is Option B.
reference: The individual partners pay tax on the income of the partnership business. They include their share of partnership income in their personal tax returns. The partnership itself is not taxed as a separate entity. It is important to note that not all partners are required to pay tax. A partner may choose not to include their share of partnership income in their personal tax return if they are not a tax resident of Australia or if they have elected not to participate in the partnership. In these cases, the other partners would be required to pay tax on the undistributed profits. (visited 02/11/2021)   (Note: Partnership is not a taxable entity, it is the partners of the partnership who pay tax on the income of the partnership. The partnership itself does not pay tax on its income. The income of the partnership is taxed to the partners who share in the profits of the business according to the partnership agreement. Each partner receives a Schedule K-1 from the partnership which reports the amount of the partnership income that the partner has been allocated and the amount of tax withheld, if any. The partner then reports this information on their individual income tax return (Form 1040).  The partnership, as an entity, does not file a federal income tax return, but it is required to file an information return on Form 1065 (U.S. Return of Partnership Income) each year with the IRS. The 1065 return is used to report the income, deductions, and other information with respect to the partnership's operations for the year. The 1065 return is not a tax return, but it is required to provide each partner with a Schedule K-1 that reports the amount of partnership income that has been allocated to the partner.
